brief.scenario: A 31-year-old man, Fergus Whitcombe, is brought after an assault. He has facial swelling, malocclusion and diplopia.
brief.task: Assess this facial-trauma presentation verbally. Explain immediate threats, a focused examination, investigations and referral. You have 9 minutes. The examiner will give findings as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Not assessing vision because “it is a fracture”.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Airway, head and cervical spine first, then vision in each eye.

grid.label: Immediate threats
grid.fail: Goes straight to the face without assessing airway, head or cervical spine.
grid.pass: Assesses airway compromise and associated head and cervical-spine injury first.
grid.high: Accounts for missing teeth and considers aspiration where relevant.

grid.label: Mandible examination
grid.pass: Assesses occlusion, mandibular movement, dentition, intraoral wounds, mental nerve sensation and facial symmetry.
grid.high: Checks for an open mandibular fracture communicating with an intraoral wound or tooth socket.

grid.label: Eye examination
grid.fail: Does not assess vision because it is “just a fracture”.
grid.pass: Documents visual acuity in each eye, pupils including a relative afferent pupillary defect, colour vision where feasible and ocular movements.
grid.high: Names the concerning findings: a tense orbit or proptosis, reduced vision, RAPD or painful restricted movements.

grid.label: Orbital compartment syndrome
grid.fail: Waits for CT or for the specialist to arrive before decompression.
grid.pass: Recognises it needs immediate assessment and emergency decompression, usually lateral canthotomy and cantholysis, by a suitably trained clinician.
grid.high: Summons ophthalmology/maxillofacial help in parallel; does not delay sight-saving treatment for CT or specialist arrival.

grid.label: Entrapment, globe injury and advice
grid.fail: Says diplopia does not matter, or measures intraocular pressure in a possible globe rupture.
grid.pass: Restricted gaze with diplopia raises concern for muscle entrapment and needs urgent specialist assessment; advises against nose blowing.
grid.high: Suspected globe rupture: protects the eye without pressure and does not measure intraocular pressure.

grid.label: Imaging and referral
grid.pass: Arranges CT of the facial bones in significant facial trauma and refers to maxillofacial surgery and ophthalmology.
grid.high: Looks for zygomatic, nasal and skull-base injury and CSF leak, without letting imaging delay sight-saving treatment.

grid.label: Antibiotics and tetanus
grid.fail: Gives routine antibiotics to every facial fracture, or misses an open mandibular fracture.
grid.pass: Gives appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis for an open mandibular fracture through the maxillofacial pathway and assesses tetanus protection.
grid.high: Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not automatically indicated for an isolated closed orbital-floor fracture.

failures.move: Waits for CT or the specialist before decompressing a suspected orbital compartment syndrome.
failures.consequence: Sight is lost. This is a critical fail.

failures.move: Does not test vision because the injury is a fracture.
Examines the face before the airway and cervical spine.

recovery.when: If you forgot the eye examination
recovery.line: I need to go back: I would document visual acuity in each eye, pupils including RAPD, and eye movements now.

knowledge.fact: Suspected orbital compartment syndrome: emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis by a suitably trained clinician, without waiting for CT or specialist arrival.
Advise against nose blowing in an orbital fracture; restricted gaze with diplopia suggests entrapment.
Open mandibular fractures (through a wound or tooth socket) need antibiotic prophylaxis via the maxillofacial pathway; isolated closed orbital-floor fractures do not automatically.

curveballs.prompt: His left orbit is now tense and his vision is falling. CT is 30 minutes away.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Do not wait: emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis by a suitably trained clinician, with help summoned in parallel.
It is a useful clue to a mandibular fracture and a measure of restoring normal occlusion.
